text:
There is a reason why grappling is the oldest and more prevalent martial art across cultures AND history. Isometric holding and grabbing is a more "primal" movement, think what babies do. Well maybe it all depends what the main occupation is in a historic culture, to throw (punches) or to grab/carry (grappling). Herding cultures probably only grab, wrangling sheep and horses and such. Agrarian societies also grab, and push. Often times a primitive plow, even when drawn by an animal, will still need the help of manpower. Hunting also uses a pull motion with a bow, if they have moved on from throwing and slings. As such, grappling is the refinement upon the motion one hones every day. Throwing/punching can be quite complex, think about the friend who you ask to throw something to you and instead unintentionally throws it in a completely ridiculous direction. Also when one gets older, you lose your speed and explosiveness but potentially your "old man strength" remains. Though in a culture that uses weapons, we are definitely back into throwing motions. To thrust and to swing, those are throwing motions.  


Wrestling allows a physical conflict to be concluded without too much damage. Winner dominates because he is on top, or not on the ground. Whereas fistfights can be a brutal fight of attrition, like you mention, or worst yet a knock out. You can't peacefully address an unpleasant person with striking, you simply beat him down. (well I guess if you're really good, you can hit the solar plexus of the chump) Quickly going to grappling range also allows you to prevent your opponent from deploying his weapons. 


Ultimately, there is always gonna be situations where striking is better than grappling. And people using prison as an contextual example is pretty wild. Prison is literally a violent free for all, like going to war alone, from things I have read. Like war, you are torturously bored but then there will be sudden instances of superviolence. text:
Boxing is good. But don't focus on a boxing match. You aren't going in the ring. Instead, be able to land a hook (right or left) when both your hands are low and you're standing a little sideways but not much, while an angry person is giving you the business.  The fastest punch you can land is your right or left hook. No wind up necessary. It's the closest to him. He will not even see it.  On the bag, or a dummy, practice that combo:  for me,  a south paw; right foot a tad forward, I'll do right hook, a looping left,  and a right cross. No straight punches. You aren't fighting Evander Holyfield, trying to get between his guard. They are loopers on the chin, jaw, to torque his head and end it as fast as possible.

When it comes to doing it thousands and thousands of times, don't worry about technique. You want those punches to be solid and thudding, using your trunk to turn, but don't even focus on that. When you do exercises like that, making sure the shots are 1) hard at the point of impact and 2) fast, your  body will optimize this for you. It takes time. 
You will be able to land such shots very hard without even thinking about it. And you get out of there. End it, leave.

text:
Do you know why a CROSS is called that ? Get both arms and form a cross ( X ) in front of your body, with the connecting point at the elbows.

The trajectory you can see is how a cross is thrown. It starts on the outside of the guard, makes inpact on centre, then continues through to finish about the opposite ear. Remember to punch through the target, not at it.

The punch witnessed here is a simple STRAIGHT RIGHT. A jab followed immeadiately by a straight right is commonly known as "the old 1 - 2"

BTW, while its good to practice your combos, you should never pre-emp what punches you'll throw in a fight. If you must, the 1-2 is as good as any, just be sure to take a step sideways immeadiately after you throw then throw again....do not step back to admire your work or to await the outcome. Capitalise on your advantage.

Simple fact is that you'll handle yourself much better if you do a bit of sparring. You have to get used to the punches coming at your head. Even getting a couple pairs of gloves and going 50% with a friend, makes a big difference.

text: Going through military training I found a lot of "tough guys" and many people want to put on gloves and test each other in that environment. It was known that I boxed and was a recreational boxer. Everyone called me out. I participated in 3 fights and just defended, using a clench or shove jab to set pace and ring control cornering my aggressor without having to hit them. An aggressive person quickly loses resolve when you successfully toy with them, and they can't control the pace and tempo of a fight. My favorite drill when I trained Muay Thai was a 3 minute drill of only being allowed to defend while the other person could use punches, elbows, kicks, and knees. If you can control a fight without throwing a punch, you can dominate one when you need to. This is the difference between an attack on the street, or  untrained fighter. A person in control doesn't need to prove it, but they certainly know how to end it.

text: I have a question I’d appreciate someone with boxing and self-defence experience answering: I hear a lot that traditional, western-style boxing is one of the best striking arts for self-defence. However, at the same time, I see *a lot of people* (many trained experts, too), talking about how different it is to punch without gloves, wraps etc… many advise palm striking, only throwing body shots with closed fists and so on. My questions are: 1. Does boxing training with gloves, using heavy bags, sparring etc actually help prepare you for a street fight? I’m not talking about the obvious outside factors such as wrestling, weapons and other fighting forms to be involved (assuming the attacker is only using fists too), but but just the fact alone that you won’t be wearing hand protection. If I can’t throw punches to the face (to avoid breaking my hands), and my overall approach has to entirely change because of it, does conventional boxing training help in a self-defence situation where I won’t have gloves? I definitely am not looking to get into fights, but I also don’t like the idea of committing a lot of time to something that potentially wouldn’t have much real-world utility. 2. Does training with wrist wraps, gloves etc still strengthen your hands, bones, ligaments etc? I understand protection is vital for volume training, but, again, I don’t like the idea that, the moment, I take those gloves off and, god forbid, I have to use my boxing for self-defence, my hands and wrists are suddenly just as vulnerable as the guy opposite me who hasn’t trained a day in his life. text:
I've been in a couple street fights growning up in the projects in New York. The fights are usually not as serious as people think they are But if given the opportunity they can go far beyond just fist and you could get seriously hurt.

What I mean by that is, usually it's a few blows exchanged and you go home but if you fall on the ground or it's ghetto types they'll jump you 1 vs 3 and stomp on you, kick you etc.

The 3 most common things I saw was wild haymaker punching, double leg grabs to try to trip you and do ground and pound like UFC or punch flailing where people just swing.

For the guys that did have some hand skill, it was usually street stand up which is not boxing per say but they know how to keep distance and weave a little. Boxing is not really needed in the average run of thw mill fight.

BUT there is a chance you're walking somewhere in some places and 3 guys try to rob you and they thought you would give it up because of the numbers disadvantage and all 3 are unarmed so start a fight.

In the case of 2 vs 1 or 3 vs 1 or encountering a guy who knows street stand up punching, boxing and grappling of some kind is best. Wrestling, BJJ, Regular JJ, Olympic wrestling, boxing, MMA, all this stuff will help. Not knowing  how to punch and grapple is a big no.

text:
It works the first 5-10 seconds if the fight starts spontaneously without any prep on either side. Which of course could end things right then and there. One good well connected punch can end everything and you no longer have an immediate problem (of course theres still fall out with police and the justice system, not to mention any backup/family the knocked out dude might have, to consider). 

However, if somebody has planned to jump you and gets in a shot, perhaps has some kind of weapon and so on then boxing training will only work in terms of your conditioning and your mental fortitude having taken blows in the past during training so you are able to process what is happening to you. Once it goes beyond those 10 seconds or once it´s a scuffle somebody else prepared for you, the outcome of actual boxing techniques will diminish in terms of efficiency. It just gets too messy, too chaotic and if the counterpart has some skills of their own and it turns into a dirty, no holds barred streetfight where anything goes, then you are better off either disengaging and running the f away or if you have to, just do whatever it takes and then run the f away.

The absolute best self defence technique ever taught to like 90+% of the entire population of humanity? Keep aware of your surroundings and run the f away at the first sign of danger. If you want to take it to next level hard mode, you will also get family, friends and complete strangers to do the same.

Don't get a false sense of security from boxing training!
The part about staying out of the street fight was the best piece of advice. 
That means use mace if you have to because if de-escalation does not work, your attacker may be armed, have you outnumbered, on drugs that make him more dangerous, etc. 
Violence on the streets isn't always macho guys testing their athleticism at a bar. They aren't boxing matches that have weight classes and rules for fairness. 
There is no such thing as a fair street fight. 
And even if you win a fight, public prosecutors may carefully check to see if they can portray you as the aggressor to win a case. Lots of good guys go to prison because they did not understand self defense laws.

text:
I’m not sure how many people are actually afraid of a physical fight—especially those with some training in combat sports. When you train regularly, you become comfortable handling altercations because it’s part of your daily routine. For example, I’m a world-level Jiu-Jitsu competitor with a background in wrestling and judo, and I’ve been training Muay Thai.

If I had to defend myself in a street fight, the person attacking me would likely get hurt pretty badly, and even though I’d just be protecting myself, I’d probably still get arrested and have to fight the court system. And most definitely, the person who attacked me would turn around and sue me civilly for damages.

What I like about training is that because we’re in these altercations multiple times a day in practice, and sparring, I’ve become very calm in any type of physical confrontation. Same with my training partners. Very chill dude’s. This naturally helps de-escalate situations because I don’t get overly tense or reactive. When you’re used to handling high-pressure scenarios, you don’t let adrenaline take over, making it easier to stay in control and prevent things from turning into an actual fight.

Would I protect my wife and my kids? Absolutely—without hesitation. But if it’s just me, I’m checking my ego at the door, and using my feet to walk away, praying they don’t grab me.

What people really fear isn’t the fight itself—it’s the aftermath: the risk of a civil lawsuit or being wrongfully arrested. Either way, I’d be looking at a long legal battle and serious out-of-pocket costs, even if I was completely in the right.

I have been nervous for many of them, especially when I was less experienced. As I got older and much more experienced, the less I felt any perceivable anxiety, which is probably not a good thing. Now that I'm well into middle age, I haven't had to fight in many years. Sometimes, I want to on rare occasions, but thankfully, the wiser me has been able to avoid it. The last time I was in a fight was with a drunk at a party I was working security at, and my hands hurt for days from punching the dude in the face multiple times. I had a hard time gripping my steering wheel for a few days. I realized that my old bones weren't able to recover as easily as they did in my youth. Thank God I made it through all of those years and fights without being seriously and permanently injured, just a lot of boxers fractures, a few concussions, a dislocated shoulder, a dislocated jaw, a bunch of black eyes, a split lip and cheek, and a few busted noses. Now, I just carry a pistol and go out of my way to avoid confrontation if at all possible.

text:
A few related tips from my personal experience to help my man:
First, and this is related to what he mentioned about mental training. I was a competitive boxer when I was younger, and I noticed that every time I would have a boxing match, I was nervous, but as soon as the actual fight stared, it (the fear) would disappear. So, I decided to harness this same reaction to work to my advantage in the street. Mentally, I would go over and over in my mind that I’m going to feel fear, it’s normal, and I accept it. After that was firmly established, I then repeatedly told myself that as soon as I feel fear, I attack. In other words, I trained my mind to use the feeling of fear itself as a trigger to attack. Most people don’t prepare themselves to deal with fear, so once they get in a legit dangerous situation, they become overwhelmed. The feeling of fear one faces in the ring is much different than the fear felt when in serious danger of losing one’s life or getting badly hurt. In such a situation, the best thing to do is preemptively strike, but many people freeze and/or panic, and that  reaction is not beneficial. However,  if you tell yourself over and over something along the lines of “if I have no choice but to defend myself, that means my only option is to fight, and the accompanying fear is my signal to attack.” Now, it is very important to attack within the first few seconds of the fear hitting. If you train this regularly, you are essentially training your body to react to the feeling of fear before you mind has a chance to start thinking. 
The above training, along with regular sparring and power training will give you confidence in your ability to defend against attacks and finish a fight.

text: I think being in excellent shape, having natural aggression, and abilities in striking and grounding yourself can do wonders for those of us who never trained. The thing about street fight is "anything" can go down. Literally anything is possible. If you're walking around in the streets, having a concealed weapon like knife won't hurt either. Street fights don't have a referee and rules. Literally anything is possible. The best way to win is to be smart enough to not hang out in shady places and if something does go down randomly, be as prepared and ready to do whatever it takes. You could be a trained fighter and still have 5 guys jump you or someone pull a gun on you or rush you with a baseball bat or a blade. You can't prepare for a street fight. You have to read the situation and react accordingly. Be smart. Avoidance is the best way to win. Don't try to play a hero unless someone else's life is in danger and even then, prioritize yourself always!

text: From my experience, you need to first know what you might be up against. I look for signs of fight training and physical stamina. I look at the ears first, then the nose, chin, forearms, and abdomen. I couldn't care less about big gym muscles. Then I test if the guy has fight training by raising my hands, rotating my body, and stepping towards the guy. If he steps back, rotates, and raises his hands, well, a conversation is the right approach because he knows how to fight and doesn't want to. For the rest, about 80% of the time, after I lead with one punch, the guy quickly wants to de-escalate. The rest of the time usually results in days of recovery from bruises, abrasions, and cuts. The best skill is to walk away, but some will not allow you to.

text: I had been training in Karate for a while and it had come to doing a bit of light (contact) sparring. Now I had zero fear - BUT - I was totally unprepared for what actually happened. When we were told to start I had a MASSIVE adrenaline rush which immediately weakened me so much I couldn't even lift my leg for a kick. I continued flat footed and with pathetic punches until the 3 minutes were over. If that had been my first street fight encounter - I would be dead. I never had that massive adrenaline rush after that first instance ever again (including real encounters). So rather than not being afraid, I would strongly suggest that beginners' put themselves in that first contact sparring position to get rid of that first debilitating adrenaline rush. Maybe you are lucky and it doesn't happen to you, but it's better to find out early under friendly conditions rather than on the street.

text: It doesn't matter what your physical level is, because if you are naturally timid, you will always be timid. I know quite a few martial arts masters who are physically excellent but are afraid of someone because they are naturally strong and also completely crazy, who are not afraid of pain, broken bones, death, anything. For example, war veterans who have been active in war zones for years, who have faced death every day and have learned to forget about pain, death, consequences in the heat of the fight, but are focused only on killing their opponent. I knew a very good kickboxing master who was a police officer in an intervention team and refused to intervene when he heard that he had to intervene against one such total lunatic, who was physically weaker than him, but was ready to kill or be killed himself. But there are also those who prefer to attack, forgetting all fear and having only one goal in front of them - to eliminate their opponent. If someone who is otherwise an excellent boxer, kickboxer or karate fighter is intimidated by this uncompromising rage, he is definitely lost from the start, because the essence is in self-confidence and focus. In addition to being excellent, we must also be aware of this excellence and gain a high degree of self-confidence so that we can coolly, calculatingly and precisely stop even such a furious monster.

text:
Fear is what keeps you alert in a street fight.
Of course if you have years of training in a martial art and you definitely know your opponent is not trained in anything then perhaps fear is not an issue.
The problem is when you do not know your opponets fighting skills and you have to be prepared for anything that can happen in a fight.
Striking sensitive areas of the body like the eyes, groin, neck etc...is an easy way to perhaps disable your opponent but come on!
You either don't fight by walking away if given the chance or if you absolutely must fight simply to prove a point (aka your ego got hurt), at the very least fight fair.
Life and death situations like a robbery or unexpected/unprovoked attack by someone towards you should be the only scenarios where what I am writing can be exempted from fair fighting.

Jab: The jab is the most basic punch in boxing and is often used to set up other punches. To perform a jab, extend your lead hand straight out in front of you, keeping your other hand up to protect your face. Your elbow should be close to your body, and your wrist should be straight. As you extend your arm, rotate your fist so that your palm faces down. Bring your hand back to your face quickly after throwing the jab.

Cross: The cross is a power punch that is thrown with your rear hand. To perform a cross, rotate your back foot and hip while extending your arm straight out in front of you. Your elbow should be close to your body, and your wrist should be straight. Rotate your fist so that your palm faces down as you extend your arm. Thanks for sharing the knowledge, heres what i learnt from this video.
1: Since im right handed i need to have a medium stance and put my left leg in the front and always be on my toes for good footwork
2: I shouldnt have my elbows on the side as then my ribs would be more visible and i should be protecting my face at all costs
JAB: simple straight punch, no flaring elbows and ur shoulders should be up so ur face doesnt get punched
CROSS: Basically a jab but with more power
HOOK: Basically a punch that forms a hook shape, again, keep your shoulders up to protect yourself
UPPERCUT: go down as if you slipped and then form a powerful upward punch

COMBOS:
1: Left jab + Left jab + Right cross
2: Left jab + right cross + left hook

🔴🔴🔴Compared to boxing, MMA often acts as a refuge for those who are not good at real fistfights and lack the courage to face their opponent in a clean stance.

Why is MMA criticized as a "sport for incompetent boxers":

Lack of boxing technique: Most MMA fighters have a loose stance and chaotic punches without a hint of elegance. Instead of technical mastery, they rely on somehow "making" their opponent "feel good" because they wouldn't survive the first round in the ring with their fists.

Choking as a sign of weakness: Khabib's win over McGregor is a perfect example of this sporting wretchedness. Khabib didn't do anything special, he didn't show any dominant sportsmanship, he just hung on to his opponent and held him until he started to tear him apart. When someone can't knock out an opponent like a man with an honest punch, they resort to this primitive hugging. It's just a desperate attempt to avoid a real fight.

Misery instead of strength: Choking is the height of embarrassment in professional sports. It seems more like the attack of aggressive lunatics on the street than the performance of a top athlete. The fact that MMA rules allow something like this only proves that this "sport" has resigned itself to any aesthetics and honor.

Killing the viewing experience: Nothing ruins a sports broadcast more than two guys rolling around on the ground in some weird knot for ten minutes. It's boring, visually off-putting, and it completely lacks the dynamism that boxing has. The viewer wants to see power and precision, not someone crawling around on the ground looking for their opponent's neck.

Conclusion: Boxing is about character and facing your opponent head-on, knowing that your skill and toughness will decide. 

MMA is just a show of cowardly tactics, where instead of fighting, you run to the ground, which makes it a poor concoction of true sportsmanship.

text:
If you get in a ring and don’t know how to avoid any technique but for punches , you gonna learn real quick. All the arts use different ranges of engagement. A fighter that only ever got punched will not be very effective at a man who has been kicking and being kicked for years will be at a further range and closing the gap has dire consequences. Equally trained I give the mma guy the win every time
  This all hinges on how the martial artist has trained compared to the boxer. A kick boxer who has only used touch training and never really been hit will be destroyed by a boxer with minimal experience because they train real time real damage where a martial artist will usually be trained to pull the power of impact as to avoid damage all together. This type of training will not suffice. 

   Provided the martial artist had engaged in training with impact like the boxer, the boxer stands no chance when equally trained. A martial artist has so many more weapons and use a range the boxer can’t comprehend. Boxers have an about 6-10 fundamental strikes in his arsenal. 

A mixed martial artist has many, many more  start with 9 basic striking weapons that can be used in an unlimited variety of ways. Additionally, beyond the addition of knees, elbow, feet ( 5 or 6 possible kicks from infinite angles) and head butts the mixed arts have take downs. Locks and submissions, finger jabs to eyes, and so much more. Mixed fighters commonly train and fight in realms that aren’t even part of boxings thinking.  Boxers have absolutely no defenses,, counters, or ways to avoid take downs. Most boxers can’t recognize or have the tools to detect an attempted take down and have absolutely no ability to defend or strike when on the ground. Knock a boxer over and he’s pretty much reduced to being a human paper weight.

   While there are boxers who have experience in other arts and ranges of fighting, here I’m addressing the arts themselves not the subjective experience of a particular individual. Once a boxer trainings in another art he becomes a mixed martial artist. 

    I’ve never said boxing is inferior nor would I ever discourage the practice there of. In my personal opinion, boxing is absolutely the best way to train a man’s hands and body to deliver the most damaging punches of all the arts. 

   Fun fact, karate as an art has absorbed boxing thru fisticuffs long before the western world adopted the art. The basic karate stance where the left arm almost looks as if held in a front block like posture and the right hand chambered at the solar plexus is the exact same posture used in fisticuffs as seen on the fighting Irish team logo. 

    Quite a few martial arts have adopted boxing for obvious reasons.

🔴🔴🔴Compared to boxing, MMA often acts as a refuge for those who are not good at real fistfights and lack the courage to face their opponent in a clean stance.

Why is MMA criticized as a "sport for incompetent boxers":

Lack of boxing technique: Most MMA fighters have a loose stance and chaotic punches without a hint of elegance. Instead of technical mastery, they rely on somehow "making" their opponent "feel good" because they wouldn't survive the first round in the ring with their fists.

Choking as a sign of weakness: Khabib's win over McGregor is a perfect example of this sporting wretchedness. Khabib didn't do anything special, he didn't show any dominant sportsmanship, he just hung on to his opponent and held him until he started to tear him apart. When someone can't knock out an opponent like a man with an honest punch, they resort to this primitive hugging. It's just a desperate attempt to avoid a real fight.

Misery instead of strength: Choking is the height of embarrassment in professional sports. It seems more like the attack of aggressive lunatics on the street than the performance of a top athlete. The fact that MMA rules allow something like this only proves that this "sport" has resigned itself to any aesthetics and honor.

Killing the viewing experience: Nothing ruins a sports broadcast more than two guys rolling around on the ground in some weird knot for ten minutes. It's boring, visually off-putting, and it completely lacks the dynamism that boxing has. The viewer wants to see power and precision, not someone crawling around on the ground looking for their opponent's neck.

Conclusion: Boxing is about character and facing your opponent head-on, knowing that your skill and toughness will decide. 

MMA is just a show of cowardly tactics, where instead of fighting, you run to the ground, which makes it a poor concoction of true sportsmanship.

text:
Well, more to it than just that.
MMA you can lose a fight without ever taking a strike and all that happened was  you got choked out which really just takes away your oxygen momentarily but ain’t gonna leave any permanent damage. Losing from a submission you recover from it SECONDS later.

Boxing you cannot lose without being hit by a strike (unless you’re DQ’d or something). 

MMA usually ends up like this: they throw a few strikes, fight goes to the ground, usually a submission, fight is over.

Boxing: punching each other in the face, grappling happens, ref tells them they gotta get each other dinner first before they can hug, separates them, they go back to punching each other in the face, someone gets knocked out. They get back up. They get knocked out again. Get back up. Only if they didn’t get back up or they got knocked out a 3rd time does it end.

It’s repeatedly doing brain damage and eating strikes.

MMA has strikes, but it also has submissions. And if they’re knocked out once that’s it. Fight over.

🔴🔴🔴Compared to boxing, MMA often acts as a refuge for those who are not good at real fistfights and lack the courage to face their opponent in a clean stance.

Why is MMA criticized as a "sport for incompetent boxers":

Lack of boxing technique: Most MMA fighters have a loose stance and chaotic punches without a hint of elegance. Instead of technical mastery, they rely on somehow "making" their opponent "feel good" because they wouldn't survive the first round in the ring with their fists.

Choking as a sign of weakness: Khabib's win over McGregor is a perfect example of this sporting wretchedness. Khabib didn't do anything special, he didn't show any dominant sportsmanship, he just hung on to his opponent and held him until he started to tear him apart. When someone can't knock out an opponent like a man with an honest punch, they resort to this primitive hugging. It's just a desperate attempt to avoid a real fight.

Misery instead of strength: Choking is the height of embarrassment in professional sports. It seems more like the attack of aggressive lunatics on the street than the performance of a top athlete. The fact that MMA rules allow something like this only proves that this "sport" has resigned itself to any aesthetics and honor.

Killing the viewing experience: Nothing ruins a sports broadcast more than two guys rolling around on the ground in some weird knot for ten minutes. It's boring, visually off-putting, and it completely lacks the dynamism that boxing has. The viewer wants to see power and precision, not someone crawling around on the ground looking for their opponent's neck.

Conclusion: Boxing is about character and facing your opponent head-on, knowing that your skill and toughness will decide. 

MMA is just a show of cowardly tactics, where instead of fighting, you run to the ground, which makes it a poor concoction of true sportsmanship.

Honestly, I agree with Joe on bare knuckle. Now that we are studying the long term effects, gloves are softer, but they rock the brain still with each strike. With bare knuckle, you're still rocking the brain, but it hurts a lot more so it's harder to ignore major damage being done in a fight, and your body encourages you to stop more (resulting in more pain, but less brain damage).

Along with that, there are also less strikes because punching someone in their skull hurts your knuckles, so you have to be more cerebral with your strikes.

text: it always annoyed me too because fighting is fighting - sure there's nothing wrong with having a preference but combat sport whether it be, boxing, kick boxing, mma, etc is great to watch when its a great fight. I think a lot of the animosity was born of ignorance. The early MMA fights were so ground fight centric and its hard to appreciate what's going on at ground level when you don't get the subtleties of the moves. Stand up fighting of any kind is pretty basic so its easy to follow, easy to appreciate. I never disliked MMA per se but now that I know a little more about grappling thanks to the great commentary and videos on youtube explaining stuff, I can actually enjoy the entire range of an MMA contest.I suppose it doesn't hurt that stand up fighting became a big part of MMA and when they changed the rules to stand the guys up from "stalemate" grappling situation - I know the purists don't like it but it makes for better entertainment and the sport is way past being about proving who has the better martial art

All the boxers are looking at MMA in terms of "what did MMA do right". I think that sport was shocked by the UFC. There are loads of MMA fans that want to see boxing matches. I watched the Olympic boxing trials every year during the 1970's and 1980's. All the new pros come out. 

We like all the fight sports. I think there should be different types of fights in the octagon. Let's see two boxers in the octagon. UFC should have some famous Muay Thai Kickboxers get out there for an exhibition. There are all kinds of fight sports. Wrestling, Kickboxing matches, I'd watch any of that in an octagon. Even the Olympic boxing is fun to watch. Olympic speed and scoring (It has to strike the white) is cool. I say put it all out there. Female MMA taught us that it is all exciting. Anyone who trains like that and fights is a superhuman. The battle ensues between two evenly matched competitors. Poetic.

Boxers get paid more money overall, but we shouldn't compare it like that. All fighters should have a plan for when they can't do this anymore. This is not like being an accountant. There are some fighters who have regular careers. Rich Franklin is a math teacher. There are a bunch of guys who were in the UFC that were higher education. text: There are a number of reasons boxing is more dangerous than ufc. A few off the top of my head are: 1) superior strikers, of course ufc has world class strikers, but they train more movements making boxers punches on average stronger. 2) focus on headshots, ufc has many ways of ending a fight. Boxing is ended by knockout and points. 3.) The 10 count is a huge problem in boxing. One knockout should end a fight. In boxing people sustain huge brain busting blows but recover within the 10 count only to recieve another. That can and has killed people. 4.) Paradoxically, boxing gloves are more dangerous than mma gloves., which are in turn more dangerous than bare knuckles. Extra padding a.) Allows the user to hit harder without injuring themselves and b,) delivers more concussive force to the brain by acting as a larger fulcrum. Cuts are not dangerous, hemotomas ond your skin are not dangerous, cranial hemotomas are life threatening. Keep in mind their are no nerves in the brain so your subjective opinion on mma gloves hurting more does not reflect the internal damage being done. All this boils down to the ufc is bloody and breaks bones, but boxing damages peoples brains waaaaay more.
